Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:1: Since we were previously engaged in the necessity of fasting for the penitent, to subdue his heart, and spoke of the things needed on a fast day, we thought fit to explain in a chapter of its own further things needed for the fast, and the things the penitent should contemplate in order to fast with a good heart and a willing soul, and to weep from the heart and soul over his sins, in order to fulfill the verse (Joel 2:12), "with fasting and with weeping and with mourning" — for when the penitent contemplates what we explained in the Gate of Fear (ch. 9) regarding the reality of sin, how much harm it causes to him, to his soul, and to the whole world, and even reaches the supernal worlds, surely he will regret with complete regret all his sins, and will see with the eye of his intellect how many deeds he must perform in order to appease the Master of all, whom he angered with his evil deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:2: Let him consider: had he sinned against a king of flesh and blood and his head were forfeit to the king, how much would he need to do to appease him! And if they told him, fast so many fasts and give so much of your money, he would give all he has for his life, as it is written (Job 2:4), "skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul" — how much more so, by an a fortiori argument, one who has sinned before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose head is forfeit to the King! And whoever says the Holy One, blessed be He, is lenient, his own life shall be forfeited leniently (Bava Kama 50b; Yerushalmi Beitzah, ch. 3, halachah 8) — rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, is patient and then collects (see Yerushalmi, ibid.), so one must appease his Creator with what will please Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:3: They explained in the Zohar (parashat Miketz 202a), in these words: and come and see, for how many generations did the Holy One, blessed be He, exact payment for the sins of the tribes — for nothing is lost before the Holy One, blessed be He, and He exacts payment from generation to generation, and judgment stands before Him always, until He exacts payment and lets the judgment rest where it is needed. From where do we know this? From Hezekiah, etc. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:4: In Sefer Chasidim (siman 344), a good parable is given for this matter, in these words: see how many fasts and weeping and supplications a person makes when his son is ill, for his soul is bitter over his son — how much more so should he do this when he has committed a transgression, which loses the good of the soul forever! — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:5: Let him consider another parable: had he a great wound that spread through the whole limb, until the physicians said, if this wound spreads and reaches the heart, he shall die — and they then command that limb to be amputated in order to save the other limbs, whose life depends on the heart. Without doubt the patient is then in great distress, crying out in pain, and no one has mercy on him — yet whatever they do to him in the way of treatment, cutting away the bad flesh and applying bandages, though harsh, is all mercy and kindness to save his life. So the penitent should compare this exactly to the matter of mortification, and see that it is necessary for him, in order to consume the filth of his inclination and subdue it, and to bring his soul to the good way — so that although he suffers, he should accept that suffering with a joyful countenance and not rebel against sufferings, as the liturgical poet said, "he shall bear the yoke and not wither, and not be disgusted by rebuke" — for if he fasts one day and suffers, he should not wither and cast off the burden of repentance from himself and say, what have I to do with this trouble, it is better for me to eat and drink — as it is said (Jeremiah 22:15), "did not your father eat and drink," etc., "then it was well with him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:6: Surely one who has not sinned has no need for fasting and mortifications, but one who has sinned needs them, as we explained above in chapter 3, and the greatest proof of this is from David the king, peace be upon him. Especially one who is afflicted with the leprosy of his sins from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, with no soundness in him — a month or two months does not suffice to consume his impurity from him; would that his whole lifetime suffice for the purification of his sins, and that they all be clean from now on without sin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:7: For a sinner sins once and it makes an imprint, and that imprint needs washing; and if before washing it he returns and repeats it, that imprint is strengthened further, and if a third time, the imprint spreads from this side to the other side, and it becomes harder to be purified — as this matter is explained in the Zohar (parashat Noach 73b), in these words: he opened and said (Psalms 51:5), "for I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me" — how much must people guard themselves from their sins before the Holy One, blessed be He! For after a person sins, his sin is marked above, and it is not erased except through great power of repentance, as it is said (Jeremiah 2:22), "though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, your iniquity is marked before Me." Come and see, once a person sins before the Holy One, blessed be He, one time, it makes a mark; when he sins a second time, that mark is strengthened further; if he sins a third time, that stain spreads from this side to that side; then it is written, "your iniquity is marked before Me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:8: Come and see, David the king — once David sinned before the Holy One, blessed be He, in the matter of Bathsheba, he thought that that sin was marked upon him forever. What is written (II Samuel 12:13)? "Also the Lord has removed your sin, you shall not die" — He removed that mark from before Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:9: He further says: come and see, David, although he confessed his sin and returned in repentance, did not remove his heart and his will from those sins he sinned, from the matter of Bathsheba — because he always feared lest one of them cause harm and accuse him at a time of danger, and therefore he never forgot them from his mind and his will. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:10: The words of this passage should enflame the heart of the penitent to perform the repentance that is proper — for it says that when a person sins even once, his sin is marked and written, as the prophet said (Jeremiah 17:1), "the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron," etc., and in the Zohar (parashat Vayechi 223b) it is explained, the matter of "the pen of iron and the point of a diamond," in these words: its "point" [tzipornah] refers to those who mention people's sins and write and mark their sins with the strength of harsh judgment, and therefore it is written, "the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with the point of a diamond [shamir]" — what is "shamir"? That which pierces stone and penetrates it on every side. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:11: Sin is erased only through the power of strong repentance, as in the manner of (Jeremiah 2:22), "though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap." It is known that the "lye" and "soap" for sin are purification through mortifications, fasts, sackcloth, and ashes, as David the king, peace be upon him, did for one sin — and if for one sin strong repentance, from lye and soap, is needed, one whose whole life has been in darkness needs how much more lye and soap, until his soul is whitened from the darkness and great blemish that darkened it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:12: For as sin enters little by little into the kelipah, until the entire stature of his soul is clothed in the kelipah, then it is said (Ezra 9:6), "for our iniquities have grown over our head" — and this is what David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 38:5), "there is no soundness in my flesh because of Your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin; for my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they are too heavy for me" — and he also said (ibid. 69:3), "I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing; I have come into deep waters, where the flood overflows me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:13: Over this the penitent should be embittered, to fast and weep and pray, and say to his soul, my soul, how have you caused me to be put to death by my own hand? Precious daughter, how have I uprooted you from the place of life and holiness to the place of death and impurity? How did I not have pity on you? Let me offer a parable: if one had unwittingly killed his beloved only son and afterward learned of it, or intentionally and regretted it, is it not fitting that he be embittered and weep over him, as our father Jacob, peace be upon him, did over Joseph, wearing sackcloth and mourning over him for many days (Genesis 37:34), which our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Bereishit Rabbah 84:20) was twenty-two years, until he was informed about Joseph? And if they told him, do such and such and you will bring him back to life, surely he would do it. So it is fitting that he be embittered to weep over what has passed, and be in mourning all his days for having killed his own precious soul — especially if he has the sin of the emission of seed in vain, for he has killed his own children — surely great mourning is called for; and he should strive to repent and pray and cast off all his transgressions from himself and be careful and alert in divine service, in order to revive his own soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:14: When he further contemplates what is explained in the Gate of Fear (chs. 7, 8), that sin is a wound in the soul, he will be embittered contemplating how many sword-wounds have struck his soul and killed it. Let him imagine, if he had several sword-wounds and was blinded in his eyes, and had his hands amputated, and was lame in his legs, and the rest of his body was full of wounds and bruises — how fitting it would be for him to weep! So he should weep over the wounds in his soul, for he is blind in his eyes, not seeing what is fitting to see, and his ears do not hear what is fitting to hear — and in this manner they said (Berachot 18b), "the wicked, in their lifetime, are called dead," for the soul in them is as though dead, and their body performs no spiritual actions — and this is what they said in the Zohar several times, "woe to human beings whose hearts are sealed, whose eyes are closed, whose ears are stopped," and the like. It follows that the sins marked in the soul are wounds and plagues, needing healing, and of this David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 41:5), "I said, Lord, be gracious to me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against You." It is good to intend this in the blessing "Heal us," regarding the illnesses of the soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:15: Further, a person should weep when he considers his death and that his soul will be seen above before the holy ones with several blemishes, and how much shame and humiliation will befall him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:16: The pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, wrote regarding the Mishnah (Avot 2:1), "and all your deeds are written in a book," in these words: he might say, behold, I am like seventy years old — "the days of our years are seventy years" — these have already been forgotten. It is not so, for "your deeds are written in a book" — and what is this book? A person's own soul — as they say, who testifies against him? His own soul, as it is said (Micah 7:5), "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom" — for in the soul are engraved the commandments and the transgressions. To what may this be compared? To a person full of wounds on his body, and his clothing covers them; when his clothing is removed, his nakedness is revealed and his shame is seen. So too, while the soul is clothed in matter, as it is said (Job 33:17), "and He hides the body from man," the blemishes of transgressions are not seen; but when matter departs from the soul, its nakedness shall be revealed, and its shame shall also be seen — woe to that shame! And this is what is said (ibid. 37:7), "He seals the hand of every man, that all men may know His work." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:17: He should also intend to weep in order to nullify the accusers accusing him, for whoever transgresses one sin acquires one accuser (Avot 4:11), and when he pictures his soul's ascent above, and how many accusers accuse it and push it away outward, it is fitting that he weep and mourn and be ashamed of his sins, and through tears his accusers are annulled, as the liturgical poet said, "I shall pour out my tears to You, wipe away my sins with my tears."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:18: Therefore it is fitting to run the tear over his forehead and his face, for there sins are marked, and in the Zohar (parashat Acharei Mot 75b) it is explained that Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosi were walking on the road, and they saw a man whose face was marked, and they said, this one has sinned; and at the end of the story they said, they said to him, who is your physician? He said to them, Rabbi Simlai. They said to him, what remedy did he give you? He said to them, the remedy of the soul, and from that day I returned in repentance, and every day I look at my face in a mirror, and I weep before the Holy One, blessed be He, who is Master of the worlds, over that sin, and with those tears I wash my face. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:19: He should intend to wash the blemish and darkness on his face through the water that descends from his eyes, just as the supernal blemish is washed through the waters of the supernal river, as explained in the Idra of Naso, in the rectifications of the supernal beard, in the second rectification (132b), where it says, and one was dark, it was washed in that light, as one who washes in that deep river, and it says afterward, what is the meaning of what you saw? They opened and said, I saw "who forgives iniquity" — end of quotation. It follows that sin is darkness and is whitened through the supernal light; so too below, in man, the darkness within him shall be washed through the waters descending from his eyes, for the gates of tears are never locked. And so they said in the Zohar (parashat Vayechi 223a): and come and see, we have learned that Leah, that righteous woman, shed many tears in order that Jacob's portion be hers, and not that wicked Esau's — this is what we have learned: any person who sheds tears before the Holy One, blessed be He, even if a punishment has been decreed upon him, it is torn up, and that punishment cannot have power over him — from where do we know this? From Leah, for it was decreed that she be Esau's portion, and she, through her supplication, preceded him to Jacob, and was not given to Esau. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:20: It seems to me that through this the verse (Psalms 6:9), "depart from me, all workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping" may be understood — the "workers of iniquity" are the outside accusing forces, and through weeping they depart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:21: Further, in the Zohar (parashat Shemot 12b), Rabbi Yehudah said: all matters of the world depend on repentance and on the prayer a person prays to the Holy One, blessed be He, and all the more so one who sheds tears in his prayer, for there is no gate through which those tears do not enter. What is written (Exodus 2:6)? "And she opened it and saw him, the child, and behold, a boy weeping" — "and she opened" — this is the Shechinah, who stands over Israel like a mother over her children, and she is always open on Israel's merit. Since she opened and saw the child — the child of delights, who are Israel, who sin before their Master in everything, yet immediately return in repentance and weep before Him like a son weeping before his father — what is written? "And behold, a boy weeping" — since he weeps, all harsh, evil decrees are broken. What is written? "And she had compassion on him." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:22: So too in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 11, 26b) it says: and when Israel would pray, all the halls would open for them; but now, in exile, of them it is said, "all the gates are locked," for the Shechinah is outside her halls, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is outside His halls, and the angels appointed over prayers are outside their halls — this is what is written (Psalms 51:17), "O Lord, open my lips" — with what shall I open it? With tears — this is what is written, "and behold, a boy weeping," immediately, "and she had compassion on him." Further, "and she opened" — when Israel open in repentance with weeping, immediately "and she had compassion on him" — surely "with weeping they shall come" (Jeremiah 31:8) — by the merit of his weeping they shall be gathered from exile — "weeping" [bechi] has the numerical value of thirty-two [lev, heart], a tear is "the daughter of the eye," a small yod, for there is a hall of tears that has no permission to open except through tears. — end of quotation. And at the end of that Tikkun it says, there is no gate open except that of tears, and what is this? "The daughter of the eye," from which the tear emerges, and of it is said (Psalms 17:8), "guard me as the apple of the eye." — end of quotation. And when he weeps, he should confess the confession written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 171).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:23: Regarding the order of fasts and repentance, how one should do this, it is written in Sefer HaKaneh, in these words: and I say to you, my son, whoever wishes to return in repentance should despair of this world, and not engage in any business of this world, and think in his heart that at every hour the King may come to him to take account of his sins, and should not eat meat nor anything that has breath in its nostrils, nor drink wine, and should sit in a fast and engage in Torah day and night, and wage war with sleep so as not to be forced to sleep the whole night, and draw all his thought to the Lord, blessed be He, and regret everything he has done, and if a transgression comes into his hand, he should push it away and distance it from himself, and his main food should be bread by weight, sufficient for his life. And he should do this: he should distance himself from the company of the world, from eating meat and wine, from any living creature, and from things that come from a living creature, and from all kinds of vegetables, and do this for forty days, and from then on the Holy One, blessed be He, will help him, and he should continue up to six years, and then he shall have no doubt whatsoever that he is a son of the World to Come, even if he eats after six years — for six years have already passed over him, corresponding to the six thousand years the world exists and the one that is desolate [the seventh millennium] — provided that from then on he is careful of transgressions that come into his hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:24: He said to me, my son, this is the excellent, true repentance, for the Holy One, blessed be He, loves a person to be subdued and humbled before Him, and to remember the day of death when he comes and goes, when he lies down and rises up, and when he walks on the road — and this is impossible with eating, drinking, and fine clothing, for the Torah says (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Yeshurun grew fat and kicked."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:25: Know, my son, that eating and drinking are all external matters, and they are good for the emanated ones outside — that is, the deniers — but for the holy, inward Israel, all their food must be with holiness, purity, and great precision. Likewise, all sexual relations are drawn after the inclination, and they are good for those who come from the side of the inclination — but the pure and clean Israel, when he comes to his wife, his intent should be for the commandments of his God, and he should seek from the Name a pure and clean soul — and then the Name sees that his intent is for good, and He emanates for him a precious, pure soul, and merits him, and also the whole world. And this intent does not come from the side of eating, drinking, and fine clothing, but only from the side of great humility.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:26: See, my son, what I did: I contemplated in my heart to repent, and I did not know how, and I sat in a fast for one hundred and twenty days, on scant bread, and nothing came into my mouth all those days except bread soaked in water, a very small amount, and every day I poured out my soul in prayer to the Name and in my studies. At the end of one hundred and twenty days Elijah, of blessed memory, came and said to me, do not afflict yourself further, my son, for the Holy One, blessed be He, has accepted your repentance; nevertheless, continue yourself for up to six years, for out of the dwelling of the God of Abraham I am with you in help. And so I did, and I did not feel all those years how they passed over me, and truly, from then on no sin or iniquity came into my hand, for the Name guarded me, and "turning from evil is understanding." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:27: In the reality of this mortification, we find that Rabbi Yishmael the High Priest did this. Rabbi Yishmael the High Priest said: I was thirteen years old when I went to Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, and I asked him, the prince of Torah, who is he and what is his name? He said to me, his name is Yofi'el. Immediately I stood and added distress upon distress, for I was in a fast, and I separated myself from all pleasures for forty days, an addition to my fast, and I said the great name at the end of forty days until I brought him down, and he descended like a flame of fire, his face like the appearance of lightning; when I saw him, I was terrified and trembled, and all my limbs came apart, and I fell backward. He said to me, son of man, what is your nature that you have shaken a great retinue? I strengthened myself and said to him, it is revealed and known before Him who spoke and the world came to be, that I did not bring you down for my own honor, but to do the will of your Master. Immediately he said to me, son of man, a foul drop, worm and maggot — how much more so your soul, since it associates with the wounded body! If so, if you wish for him to be revealed to you, sit forty days in a fast, and immerse twenty-four times each day, and do not taste anything filthy, nor any kind of legume or vegetable, and do not gaze at a woman, and sit in a dark house — and do this, and he taught him the Name, and taught, and he [the angel] would ascend and descend.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:28: Although the pious and holy author of Sefer HaKaneh, peace be upon him, exaggerated in his order of repentance, not every person can fulfill it — especially a pampered person who has grown up all his life in pleasure — if he is uprooted all at once to perform this mortification, he might become ill; therefore one must conduct himself gradually, little by little, in the ways of repentance — such as beginning to abstain from meat and wine, which is called "affliction," as we find Daniel, peace be upon him, did, as it is said (Daniel 10:3), "I ate no delightful bread, and no meat or wine came into my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil" — and they said in Tractate Yoma (76b), on this verse: from where do we know that anointing is called "affliction"? As it is written, "I ate no delightful bread, and meat and wine did not come into my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil," etc. — what is "I ate no delightful bread"? Rav Yehudah the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat said in the name of Rav, he did not eat warm bread of pure wheat. From where do we know this is considered affliction? As it is written (Daniel 10:12), "and he said, do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself," etc., "your words were heard; and I have come because of your words, for you are delightful [chamudot]." — end of quotation. Rashi explained "chittei dechayta" as fine, clean wheat, as we translate "the delightful garments of Esau" as "dechayta" — end of quotation. Here, all these things mentioned in the verse are considered some degree of affliction, and anointing, because he did not anoint himself at all, is the greatest affliction of all — for if you say that affliction applies only to anointing alone, why is it mentioned in the verse, and moreover, why did the Gemara need to explain what "delightful bread" is? Rather, surely this is to inform us that abstaining from delightful bread is also called affliction. In this manner, one who has not been accustomed to affliction should begin gradually to accustom himself to subdue his inclination little by little.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:29: So too our sages, of blessed memory, explained in Midrash Yelamdenu, on (Ezekiel 36:26), "and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh" — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel, remove the evil inclination gradually, as it is said (Isaiah 62:10), "pave, pave the highway, clear it of stones" — and in the World to Come I will uproot it, as it is said, "and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:30: So too Rabbeinu Bachya, the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot, wrote (end of Gate of Love), in these words: proceed gradually and calmly in acquiring the good attributes, as much as your circumstances can bear, and be careful of excess and going beyond without gradation, lest you be lost — for too much oil in a lamp causes its light to be extinguished; be careful of neglect, laziness, and slackness, and cling to alacrity with alacrity. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:31: Anything a person does in accepting sufferings to afflict his soul shall be counted for him as repentance — for Ahab, since he was accustomed to eating at the third hour, ate instead at the seventh hour, etc., as we quoted the words of our sages, of blessed memory, in chapter 3. This is the gradation for acquiring fasting: he shifts himself from eating at the hour he was accustomed to, until, when he does fast, it will not be hard for him; and afterward he should accustom himself to fast one day a week, until he accustoms himself to Monday and Thursday, and afterward accustoms himself to a third day, until he accustoms himself throughout the whole week to fast without it being difficult — for habit is dominant in everything, and it becomes second nature.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:32: He should accustom himself to fast one day with its night, for they said in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Zuta, ch. 4) that Israel fasted forty days, and on the last day they lodged in a fast, and Yom Kippur was fixed as a fast on which we cease eating while it is still day, in these words: in parashat Ki Tissa, the forty days Moses ascended to the heights to bring the Torah to Israel, they were accustomed to observe fasting and affliction all those days, and on the last of them all they decreed a fast and lodged in a fast. And it concludes further on that that day was fixed for atonement for Israel until the end of all generations.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:33: When he has accustomed himself to interrupt [eating] a day and its night, he should accustom himself to fast two days and two nights — which later authorities wrote is equivalent to forty days [of merit] without being consecutive, though I have received that it is equivalent to twenty-seven consecutive [days] — and all this a person should accustom himself to, by shifting himself from eating at the hour he was accustomed to, delaying past the accustomed hour by two or three hours, even on a day he fasted, so that he not feel the interruption on the second night — until he becomes accustomed to the repentance that the pious author of Sefer HaKaneh, peace be upon him, wrote, until his repentance ascends to the Throne of Glory, where the World to Come is, and the World to Come has neither eating nor drinking; and since he holds fast to repentance, which is in the World to Come, he must grasp its attributes, which are abstinence from the matters of this world — from eating, drinking, anointing, and other pleasures. For this reason Yom Kippur is forbidden with five afflictions, corresponding to the supernal heh, which is the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:34: So too we find in the first chapter of Ta'aniyot (1:6), that when they decreed three fasts upon the community and they were not answered, they decree three more fasts, which are forbidden in eating, drinking, washing, anointing, etc., like the fast of Yom Kippur — to indicate that the complete repentance to ascend to the World to Come consists of these mentioned. And if an individual wishes to do this one day a week for the atonement of his sins in this order, happy is he.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:35: So too the prophet taught us that the grades of repentance, up to ascending to the Throne of Glory, are these mentioned in the verse (Joel 2:12), "and return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting and with weeping," etc. — and it says "to Me [adai]" in the manner our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Yoma 86a), on "return, O Israel, to the Lord your God" (Hosea 14:2), great is repentance, for it reaches to the Throne of Glory.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:36: I heard in the name of our master Rabbi Isaac Luria Ashkenazi, peace be upon him, that the word "TeShuVaH" [repentance] alludes to the grades needed for it, being an acronym for "Ta'anit" [fasting], "Sak" [sackcloth], "vaEfer" [and ashes], "Bechiyah" [weeping], "Hesped" [mourning]. And although sackcloth is not mentioned in this verse, this is because it is mentioned in the Torah through Jacob and the Prophets, as we explained above. And it may be that it is included within "mourning," for one who mourns his dead grieves and wears sackcloth and ashes, as our father Jacob, peace be upon him, did, and it is likewise mentioned in the Scroll of Esther (4:3), "and in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and mourning; sackcloth and ashes were spread out for many."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:37: Whoever is ill and cannot fulfill all these, but fulfills some of them, is still called "repentance" — the proof being King Hezekiah, peace be upon him, of whom what is mentioned (II Kings 20:2-3) is weeping and prayer, not fasting and sackcloth, because he was ill, and he was answered in his prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:38: One of the things the penitent must do is to pray over his sins to the Holy One, blessed be He, that He forgive him, and so it is explained in Midrash Tehillim, on the psalm "when he comes to him" [Bathsheba episode], in these words: from here you learn that whoever knows he has sinned and prays over the sin and fears it, and negotiates it between himself and the Omnipresent — the Holy One, blessed be He, forgives him. And whoever knows he has sinned yet tramples with his feet and removes it from before his eyes, the Holy One, blessed be He, demands it from him — and so it says (Psalms 49:6), "why should I fear in days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels surrounds me" — those who extinguish [their sins] beneath their heels, etc. — so whoever removes his sin from before his eyes, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not forgive him; therefore David said (ibid. 51:5), "and my sin is ever before me." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:39: In the Zohar (parashat Vayechi 243b), on the verse "Dan shall be a serpent by the way, a viper by the path" (Genesis 49:17), it says, in these words: Rabbi Yitzchak said, Dan is the serpent, lurking on roads and paths — and should you say this refers to Samson, so too above there is a small serpent, gatherer of all the camps, lurking on roads and paths, afterward [gathering] hosts and camps — and from here emerge those who lie in wait for people regarding sins they have cast behind their shoulders. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:40: It is also a positive commandment for the penitent to confess his sin, as it is said (Numbers 5:7), "and they shall confess their sin which they have done." The order of confession is "chatati, aviti, pashati" [I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed], and their secret is explained in parashat Vayikra (Zohar 20a), on the verse "against You alone have I sinned." It is customary to confess in alphabetical order, because through the twenty-two letters all the worlds were created, as explained in Sefer Yetzirah, and through sin all the worlds are blemished; therefore it is fitting to confess in alphabetical order.
